interactions.summary: A student asks whether Jiang's account of will resembles Nietzsche's will to power. Another student connects it to psychological self-efficacy, and Jiang answers yes to both lines by recasting the idea as manifestation: willing a reality into being.

Jiang extends the comparison by saying these frameworks imply that the universe is fundamentally about will rather than about ready-made categories of good and evil, though he flags the idea as strange and still to be unpacked.

When a student asks whether Piccarda simply did not want escape or ascent badly enough, Jiang restages the scene from inside the convent and asks the class to inhabit her emotional state. A student answers with fear, despair, and prayer for divine rescue, while also suggesting the prayer may have lacked force.

speaker_notes.note: The psychology reference is clearly to self-efficacy, but the ASR garbles the theorist's name. Keep the concept, not the spelling, as the stable content.

claims.claim: Students explicitly compare Jiang's account of will to Nietzsche's will to power and to the psychology concept of self-efficacy, and Jiang treats those comparisons as basically right.
Jiang says the popular word for this process is manifestation: one imagines an outcome because one has first willed it into being.
Jiang argues that the shared point behind these models is that the universe is fundamentally structured by will rather than by intrinsic categories of good and evil.
A student asks whether Piccarda's problem was simply that she did not want escape or ascent badly enough, and Jiang accepts that as the right pressure point to investigate further.
Jiang reconstructs Piccarda's predicament as a live emotional scene inside the convent, pushing the class to ask what fear, despair, and prayer would have felt like under armed coercion.
A student suggests Piccarda would have been in despair, unable to face the soldiers directly, and praying for God to save her, while hinting that the prayer may not have been strong enough.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang compresses Nietzsche, self-efficacy, and his own Dante reading into one popular word: manifestation.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It shows him translating a dense philosophical comparison into a contemporary keyword the class already recognizes.

signature_moments.moment: The moral universe is recast as will all the way down, with good and evil demoted beneath the force of willing.
signature_moments.source_phrase: there's really no good and evil in the universe there's just will
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's most provocative metaphysical claim and one of the sharpest formulations likely to matter later for lens work.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang stops abstract theorizing and drops the class back inside the convent door with soldiers outside, forcing them to imagine Piccarda's fear in real time.
signature_moments.source_phrase: soldiers come to you ... what is she thinking
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves Jiang's method of testing a theory of will by re-entering the emotional texture of the coercive scene.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The psychology comparison students use for Jiang's view that believing you can do something is itself a major cause of accomplishing it.
Jiang's preferred popular label for willing an imagined reality into concrete existence.

chronology_notes.note: The packet first broadens Jiang's will-language into cross-framework comparisons with Nietzsche and psychology, then returns that theory to Piccarda by reconstructing her inner emotional state at the moment of coercion.

uncertainty_notes.note: The self-efficacy theorist's name is garbled by ASR, and the end of segment 0432 is cut off. Keep the stable comparisons to self-efficacy and to not-strong-enough prayer without overclaiming the missing words.
